newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close higher, Fed coupon pass helps.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close higher, Fed coupon pass helps.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries shook off morning doldrums to end higher on Wednesday, boosted by a Federal Reserve coupon pass operation and economic news pointing to a continued benign inflation environment.
The 30-year bond was at 99-6/32, up 14/32 in late trading. Its yield fell to 6.69 percent from 6.72 percent. The two-year note was up 2/32 at 100-14/32 to yield 6.01 percent.
"The market keeps getting nothing but good news," said Dave Connors, head trader at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.

Treasuries were depressed and posted thin volumes for most of the morning, until the Fed surprised the market late morning by buying $1.6 billion in coupons. Traders said the market had anticipated the coupon pass, but not such a large size.
"The coupon pass was clearly the catalyst to the day," said Pat Alexander, head trader at BancAmerica Securities Inc. "The $1.6 billion is a healthy chunk of securities."
Wednesday's Fed pass was the second of a likely four tranche coupon pass and the expectation of two more operations should keep an underlying bid in the market, traders said.
Treasuries rose as much as 10/32 after the coupon pass and on reported buying from retail accounts and Asian and European central banks, traders said.

Gains were extended after the Fed released its Beige Book report. It told of continued economic expansion in May and early June, but with pockets and weakness, as well as a tight labor market that is producing little or no wage pressures.

At about the same time, Fed Governor Susan Phillips acknowledged that a number of factors, such as slow growth abroad and high productivity, have helped keep inflation low. She noted that the buildup in wages has not translated into higher prices.
Phillips' remarks were later echoed by Boston Fed President Cathy Minehan.

"No one said anything that was new," said Alexander. "And the fact (the Beige Book and the Fed officials) didn't say anything negative, especially on inflation ... ratified the market's existing levels, and the notion of no July tightening and that the possibility of an August tightening looks increasingly questionable."
The bullish attitude pushed Treasuries back to their highs, a feat seen a few times the past week.
"But we failed to break through them," Connors said.

"The two-year seems like it doesn't want to go through 6.0 percent and the 10-year has resistence at 6-3/8 percent," he added. "The only thing holding us back is where we are relative to (fed) funds."
Traders said the market will not accept a spread of below 50 basis points between the two-year note, currently at 6.01 percent, and the 5.50 percent funds rate.

"The Fed is still biased to tighthening; we have tight labor markets and capacity constraints," Connors said, noting that two-years below 6.0 percent would suggest the market expects an ease. To talk of an ease is premature, he said.
Also helping the market, traders said, was the Treasury's announcement that it was cutting the size of next week's two- and five-year note auctions.
Treasury will sell $15.5 billion of two-year notes, a $1.0 billion reduction from the last auction. It also cut the size of the five-year note sale by $500 million to $11.5 billion.
Some players warned that with the Fed not out of the picture, there could be significant concessions ahead of next Tuesday and Wednesday's auctions.
In the meantime, the market looks to the Philadelphia Fed's June business outlook survey, due Thursday morning.

As of 1500 EDT, trading volume was $70 billion, 5 percent below an average Wednesday in the second quarter, according to GovPX. Bill volume was 18 percent below average, while coupon volume was average.
Five-year notes rose 4/32 to 100-29/32 to yield 6.28 percent and the 10-year note was up 8/32 to 101-21/32 to yield 6.39 percent.
Three-month bill rates were up one basis point at 4.93 percent, six-month rates were down two basis points at 5.07 percent and year bill rates were down one basis point at 5.33 percent.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
